summary: Deep dive into KV cache eviction and paging behavior observed in Polaris ML long-context workloads. Discussed root causes (memory pressure, sharded cache alignment, prefix reuse inefficiencies), mitigation (tuning cache size/pinning, eviction policies, workload-aware batching) and next steps to reproduce and benchmark on a dedicated test cluster. Also touched on on-prem networking and quantization impacts on cache size and latency.
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Park: okay everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood. we have Maya on the call and Luis. can we do quick intros?
00:10 Elena Ruiz: sure I'm Elena, CTO at Polaris ML, and Tom is our eng lead, Priya is ML eng working on long-context doc ingestion. Samir handles infra.
00:22 Maya Singh: hi all, SE at Redwood, I'll start with an overview then dive into the kv cache traces you shared. quick agenda: symptoms, traces, reproduction, mitigations, next steps.
00:35 Tom Chen: symptoms are eviction spikes and latency tail at around 1.2 to 1.5s per request for long sequences, throughput drops under load. also seeing increased paging on nodes.
00:47 Priya Kapoor: we load many long docs with prefixes reused across requests, so we expect high prefix hit rates but it's not matching.
00:58 Luis Ortega: from the traces you sent we saw high cache churn; keys being evicted and re-populated within 2-3 requests. that suggests memory pressure or mismatched sharding.
01:12 Samir Patel: note we're running on prem: 4x A100 equivalent, with a private VPC and NFS-backed model store. some nodes showed swap activity which is surprising.
01:26 Maya Singh: ok that helps. first question: are you using quantized model builds in that cluster or FP16?
01:34 Priya Kapoor: we're using q4_0 builds for cost. we also have some mixed instances for higher throughput.
01:40 Jordan Park: quick flag: quantization reduces memory for weights but the kv cache still scales with sequence length and per-token memory, so q4 doesn't avoid large kv usage.
01:52 Tom Chen: we also noticed eviction aligns with peak batch injection from our batching layer. could batching be causing kv overcommit?
02:01 Maya Singh: yes, batching can spike concurrent contexts which temporarily increase required kv cache capacity. if autoscaling or room for cache isn't provisioned, system evicts older contexts.
02:12 Elena Ruiz: what's typical eviction policy in your runtime? LRU? something custom?
02:18 Luis Ortega: our runtime uses an LRU-ish policy with segment-level pinning for active contexts; but when shard alignment isn't correct, the per-shard LRU can evict hot prefixes.
02:29 Priya Kapoor: shard alignment? can you explain?
02:32 Luis Ortega: each GPU holds a shard of the kv cache. if requests for a given prefix route across different shards (for example due to round-robin routing or model replica mismatch), the prefix won't be reused in the same shard and caching benefits drop, leading to more population and eviction.
02:50 Tom Chen: we do have a round-robin upstream balancer; we thought prefix reuse was preserved at the request layer but perhaps not.
02:59 Maya Singh: that's a common issue: smart routing needs to pin consistent keys to the same cache shard or use a shared cache layer. without that, you get high churn.
03:12 Jordan Park: also paging you mentioned could be OS-level swap or device-level GPU memory swapping if memory exceeds GPU RAM and there's fallback to host. Samir, you said swap activity on nodes?
03:23 Samir Patel: yes, vmstat shows some swap in peaks; we assumed it was IO from NFS but could be kernel shuffling.
03:30 Maya Singh: swapping is catastrophic for latency; needs to be eliminated for SLOs. we recommend setting strict memory cgroups, avoid host swap, and ensure eviction happens before swap rather than after.
03:44 Priya Kapoor: what about prefix reuse semantics? we see repeated headers of docs being reused across ingestion. how to ensure those stay in cache?
03:53 Luis Ortega: you can pin frequent prefixes (pin policy) or increase per-shard cache allocation for those hot contexts, or enable shared KV segments for small prefix sets. also increase cache TTL for pinned contexts.
04:06 Tom Chen: is pinning supported in hosted and private runtimes?
04:10 Maya Singh: yes, both — on private we provide config knobs: per-model cache size, pin lists, eviction thresholds, and routing policies (consistent hashing) to keep prefixes on same shard.
04:22 Elena Ruiz: about consistent hashing — do you have examples of configs?
04:26 Maya Singh: we'll share a recommended config; quick note: consistent_hash=prefix_id mod num_shards is simplest, but you need sticky routing at the load-balancer layer as well.
04:39 Priya Kapoor: another symptom: we see TTL-based eviction even though contexts are active. is there a race between active usage and TTL refresh?
04:49 Luis Ortega: yes if your activity windows are smaller than eviction intervals and the refresh isn't recorded epoch-ly, you can lose the TTL. ensure access updates LRU timestamps and consider heartbeat touch for very small windows.
05:02 Jordan Park: want to call out quantization interplay: smaller model memory sometimes tempts you to pack more replicas per GPU; that increases concurrent contexts per GPU and leads to higher kv stress. packing density needs to consider kv capacity not just weight memory.
05:20 Tom Chen: good point, we did increase replicas after quantizing and saw the problem surface.
05:26 Maya Singh: paging is also influenced by GPU kernel selection and memory alloc patterns. using fused attention kernels helps reduce transient memory spikes; kernel graph compilations that pre-allocate KV buffers avoid frequent device allocations.
05:39 Priya Kapoor: we also saw spikes when sequence length suddenly jumps (user sends a long doc). how to handle long-context bursts gracefully?
05:48 Luis Ortega: we have a few strategies: 1) dynamic pre-allocation for expected max sequence length with admission control; 2) prefix summarization (store condensed KV for very long prefixes); 3) partial eviction with on-demand paging to host as a last resort with local SSD backing.
06:05 Samir Patel: local SSD backing for kv paging — does Redwood support that in private deployment?
06:11 Maya Singh: yes, we support local NVMe-backed paging policies; in most cases we advise avoiding host paging for latency SLOs but NVMe can be a lower-latency fallback vs networked NFS.
06:24 Priya Kapoor: you mentioned prefix summarization — is that lossy? does it impact quality?
06:29 Luis Ortega: it can be lossy; tradeoff is lower memory vs some contextual fidelity. we typically summarize very old prefixes or use learned summaries (condense embeddings) and keep that for long-term context. test with your eval prompts to see quality impact.
06:44 Jordan Park: let's go through the concrete repro steps we need from you: micro-benchmarks, representative request traces with routing headers, and your load balancer config. we also want kernel logs and dmesg around the time of evictions.
06:55 Tom Chen: we can provide request traces; what micro-benchmarks do you want?
07:00 Maya Singh: a small harness that floods the cluster with your long-context patterns: high prefix reuse vs unique prefixes, varying sequence lengths (1k, 4k, 16k), and controlled batching concurrency. we'll provide the harness.
07:12 Priya Kapoor: ok we'll run it, Priya will take action.
07:18 Jordan Park: in parallel we'll provision a short-lived dedicated test cluster with pinned routing to try to reproduce without round-robin interference.
07:26 Elena Ruiz: any quick config changes we can try today to stop paging?
07:30 Maya Singh: set vm.swappiness=0, disable swap on hosts, ensure cgroup memory limits for the runtime are set so it evicts before kernel swap, increase per-shard kv capacity if you have spare GPU memory, and ensure consistent routing sticky hashing.
07:46 Samir Patel: noted, we'll set swappiness and check cgroups.
07:50 Tom Chen: question on metrics — what should we monitor to catch early signs?
07:54 Luis Ortega: monitor per-shard kv occupancy, evictions/sec, cache hit rate for prefixes, GPU memory headroom, vmstat swap in/out, and latency p95/p99. Redwood console exposes token-level cost and per-route cache metrics.
08:10 Priya Kapoor: latency p99 is our SLO — when cache churns p99 jumps from 450ms to >1s.
08:17 Jordan Park: right, and you'll see correlation between evictions/sec and p99.
08:21 Elena Ruiz: any cautions around quantization and kernel choices? we use q4_0 but may try q5_x soon.
08:28 Maya Singh: newer quant formats can change memory layout and kernel preference; some kernels handle q5 better. always run your kernel benchmark for your sequence distribution — kernel selection can change transient memory. we'll share our kernel selection checklist.
08:43 Tom Chen: network impact: we have a VPC with private peering to storage. could that cause delayed cache populates?
08:50 Maya Singh: yes, if model artifacts or page-ins hit NFS over the network during populate it increases latency. we prefer local NVMe for model artifacts under heavy populate churn.
08:59 Priya Kapoor: what's the recommended eviction threshold? like keep below 70% occupancy?
09:06 Luis Ortega: 65-80% depending on burstiness; lower for highly bursty workloads. also ensure headroom for a worst-case concurrent contexts estimate.
09:16 Jordan Park: wrapping up, we'll share a tuning guide, the micro-benchmark harness, and provision the repro cluster. Priya and Samir will run host-level changes and gather logs.
09:29 Elena Ruiz: sounds good, thanks. any blockers?
09:33 Tom Chen: none, timeline looks fine.
09:35 Jordan Park: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in the next steps and send the docs.
09:40 End of recording
notes_topics: KV cache eviction causes (memory pressure, sharding, routing)
Paging vs swap and host-level mitigations
Batching impact on concurrent KV usage
On-prem considerations: NVMe vs NFS, cgroups, swappiness
